name: Papier poudre blotting sheets

card.summary: Thin sheets of paper coated with fine face powder that are pressed to the skin to remove shine and deposit a light matte finish.
card.note: Effect is temporary; shine returns as skin produces oil.

quick.overview:
Papier poudre, or powder papers, are small sheets carried in a booklet. Each is pressed onto the face to take up oil and leave a thin layer of powder. Pressing them onto the forehead, nose and chin reduces shine without a compact or makeup brush.

They date to the early twentieth century, when carrying them in a handbag was a discreet way to refresh makeup in public.
quick.how: People blot the shiny areas of the face through the day, usually the T-zone, then carry on. Because the paper carries powder, it also touches up makeup.
quick.risks: No notable risks. Powder tints can mismatch skin tone, and people with sensitive skin may react to fragrance or pigments in some products.

lead: Papier poudre (powder papers) are thin sheets coated with fine face powder, sold in pocket booklets and pressed to the skin to take up surface oil and leave a light matte finish. People use them to keep the forehead, nose and chin from looking shiny in person or in photographs, and to refresh makeup through the day without a compact or brush. They differ from plain oil-blotting papers such as aburatorigami in that the sheet itself carries powder.[1]

The format dates to the early twentieth century. A museum record credits the maker Lehcaresor with first producing Papier Poudré in 1903.[1] Powdered leaves let wearers touch up in a handbag-sized format without a compact or mirror.
Booklets are sold in several tints for different skin tones.[1] No published studies have tested them.

chain: Sheet is pressed onto oily areas
Light powder leaves a matte finish
angle.text: Pressing a sheet on the T-zone lifts oil and leaves a thin layer of powder, so skin looks matte in person and in photos and makeup is refreshed without a mirror or brush.

infobox: Tinted editions for different skin tones[1]

paras: Each sheet is a thin paper impregnated with powder. It is pressed, not rubbed, onto the skin. A museum-held booklet of the product contains 65 leaves and is packaged in a small card cover with a hook for hanging.[1]

The packaging describes the leaves as absorbing oil and shine and also setting makeup and freshening the face and hands.[1] The powder color varies by edition: one catalogued range offers a fair-skin edition, a very fair edition and a rose edition for medium to dark skin.[1]

The V&A record lists Lehcaresor as the originator of Papier Poudré, first made in 1903, and a British company later repackaged the product around 2002.[1] The format suited an era when portable compacts were uncommon and reapplying makeup in public was considered improper.

Sheets are used on the T-zone, the forehead, nose and chin, where oil collects. Because the paper carries pigment, one pass both removes shine and leaves a thin matte layer, which people use before photos or meetings or to refresh foundation midday.[1]

timeline.event: Lehcaresor first produces Papier Poudré, per a museum record.[1]
A British company repackages the product, per the museum record.[1]
